Pumpjacks operating in Kern County, which has a long history of oil production, in California’s 22nd Congressional District on Oct. 16, 2026 near Bakersfield, California. Mario Tama | Getty Images Oil prices climbed Thursday on worries over a possible escalation in the Middle East conflict as the U.S. reportedly plans to resume strikes against Iran. Brent crude Add To Watchlist futures rose 1.71% to $110.67 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate Add To Watchlist crude gained 1.42% to $98.53. The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, The New York Times reported, citing unnamed U.S. officials. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said. The U.S. has also ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets, after reports said that the U.S. had directed some staff in the wider Gulf region to leave. The economic fallout from elevated oil prices, however, may be less severe than in previous decades, as consumers have become less vulnerable to energy shocks, according to David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors. "$100 oil today is very different than $100 oil, you know, 20, 30 years ago," Wagner said, noting that crude prices remain well below their inflation-adjusted historical highs. He pointed to U.S. government data showing that gasoline accounted for roughly 5% of the average American's disposable income a decade ago, compared with about half that today, suggesting households may be better positioned to withstand elevated energy costs. "I think we can hold that umbrella over our head ... from the rainstorm of oil," he said. *— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.*

items.title: Judge rules against DHS's policy of knocking on doors to track down possible noncitizen voters - CBS News
items.excerpt: A federal judge ruled late Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act. The ruling took aim at an operation that was documented by a CBS News investigation earlier Wednesday. Homeland Security Investigations has posted photos and videos of agents approaching homes in multiple states. The Trump administration says the practice is part of an effort to crack down on voting by noncitizens, but critics say it could intimidate legal voters. In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin ordered federal immigration authorities to stop carrying out "elections-related field operations and field interviews" in nine states, including California and New York, if the operations are likely to involve people who government officials "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens." Her order will remain in effect until polls close on Election Day. She stayed the ruling until 5 p.m. on Friday, which will give the government a chance to seek appeal. Martinez-Olguin sided with groups that sued over the noncitizen voting investigation surge, including the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United. She found the policy likely ran afoul of a section of the Voting Rights Act that makes it illegal to "intimidate, threaten, or coerce" those who assist people with voting or engage in voter mobilization efforts. "Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections," the judge wrote. "Rather, Plaintiffs seek to stop DHS from continuing to investigate U.S. citizens, who have a legal right to vote, in a way that intimidates and threatens the participation of CNA/NNU members from urging or aiding others to vote."

In Texas, early voting is up 74% compared with 2022. In Kansas it’s more than doubled. Maine, North Carolina and Ohio also have seen increases of more than 30% in early in-person and mail voting compared with the same point in 2022. Democrats are trying to flip Republican-held Senate seats in each of those states. In most of them, Republicans are accounting for a smaller share of advance voters than they did four years ago. The AP’s data, which runs through Tuesday, gives a snapshot of potential voter enthusiasm — and where it might be lacking — after early voting has opened in most states during a midterm cycle that has shifted in often unpredictable ways. items.title: In New Mexico governor's race, Deb Haaland's historic bid ...
items.excerpt: ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. – If Deb Haaland wins New Mexico’s race for governor this year, she’ll make history as the first Native American woman to lead a state. But first she has to convince New Mexicans that they should keep Democrats in charge. The state persistently ranks near the bottom nationally on poverty, crime and public education, and disenchanted voters are pleading for change. A loss would be embarrassing for Democrats, who hold all the top state offices and have controlled the Legislature nearly continuously for almost a century. Haaland blames President Donald Trump for compounding the state's problems by cutting social programs that New Mexicans disproportionately rely on and increasing the cost of living by waging war against Iran. She proposes expanding existing tax credits and spending more on safety net programs to help families make ends meet. Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo in west-central New Mexico, once relied on government assistance as a single mother. She rose through the ranks, serving in Congress for two years before being tapped as President Joe Biden’s interior secretary.

The ruling stems from a lawsuit arguing that DHS’s so-called Unlawful Voter Initiative — an operation launched amid the ongoing midterm election — included aggressive and illegal efforts like “deploying armed and often militarized agents to homes to interrogate residents about whether they are eligible to vote.” ... items.excerpt: Chris Pratt Confirms Star-Lord Will Return to the MCU ... # Chris Pratt Confirms Star-Lord Will Return to the MCU, Says ‘Hard Action’ Has Been Taken to Make It Happen ... Good news, “ Guardians of the Galaxy” fans. Chris Pratt, who has played superhero Star-Lord across six films, recently confirmed that his character will return to the MCU and that the studio has already taken “hard action” to make it happen. ... “I have a great relationship with Kevin [Feige] and Lou [D’Esposito], and there have been both ongoing conversations about how we make good on that promise and also hard action taken to make sure that we make good on that promise,” said Pratt on The Playlist’s “Bingeworthy” podcast while discussing Star-Lord’s comeback. He continued: “So yeah, you’ll see Star-Lord again, which is very exciting, but I’m not at liberty to say when that’s going to be, but he’s not going anywhere.” ... The news comes months after Pratt admitted he pitched Marvel an idea for bringing Star-Lord back into the MCU. “I’m happy to do anything they want me to do and will,” Pratt said about Marvel when on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast. “And also, I personally have a really strong vision of what I would want him to do. And I think it’s fucking great.” ... The next installment in the MCU, “Avengers: Doomsday,” hits theaters on Dec. 18.

items.title: Telemundo Gears Up for Latin Music's Biggest Night: The 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards to Air Live Thursday, October 22 - NBCUniversal Telemundo Enterprises Press Releases
items.excerpt: Telemundo Gears Up for Latin Music's Biggest Night: The 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards to Air Live Thursday, October 22 - NBCUniversal Telemundo Enterprises Press Releases ... # Telemundo Gears Up for Latin Music’s Biggest Night: The 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards to Air Live Thursday, October 22 ... WHAT: Telemundo and Billboard announced the date for the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards, the longest-running and most prestigious awards show in Latin music. The live music special will bring fans together for an unforgettable celebration of Latin music’s biggest stars, honoring the year’s top artists, albums, and songs, while featuring exciting live performances from today’s top music talent. The Billboard Latin Music Awards is the only awards show to honor the most popular albums, songs, and performers in Latin music, as determined by the actual sales, streaming, radio airplay and social data that informs Billboard’s weekly charts during a one-year period. WHEN: Thursday, October 22 ... WHERE: The award show will take place at the James L. Knight Center in Miami, Florida, and will be available LIVE on Telemundo and Peacock. The awards will coincide with Billboard Latin Music Week, which returns to Miami October 19-22, celebrating Latin music, culture, and entertainment all week long with exclusive performances, one-of-a-kind conversations, workshops, showcases and exclusive fan experiences. Learn more about Billboard Latin Music Week at billboardlatinmusicweek.com.
